passages: A conversation is made of turns. Each turn holds a message and the time at which it was received. Earlier turns stay in the conversation after new ones arrive. The order of the turns follows the order in which they were sent.

Messages are made of characters. A message can be short, with a few words, or long, with several paragraphs. Some messages contain lists, tables or blocks of code. Others contain plain sentences without any particular structure.

An attachment is a file that arrives together with a message. Attachments have a name, a size and a type. Common types include text files, spreadsheets, documents and images. The content of an attachment is separate from the text of the message itself.

Dates can be written in several ways. The same day may appear as a full date with the month spelled out, or as a sequence of numbers separated by dashes or slashes. In some regions the day comes before the month, and in others the month comes first.

Time zones divide the world into regions that share the same clock time. The offset of a time zone is measured from Coordinated Universal Time. Some regions change their offset during part of the year. Two events written with different offsets can describe the same moment.

A number can be written with digits or with words. Large numbers are often grouped in blocks of three digits. The character used to separate those groups differs between regions, and so does the character that separates the whole part from the decimal part.

A list is a sequence of items. The items of a list can be marked with bullets, with numbers or with letters. A list can contain a single item or many. Some lists contain other lists, which gives them several levels.

A table arranges values in rows and columns. The first row often holds the names of the columns. Each cell sits at the meeting point of one row and one column. A table can have empty cells where no value was recorded.

Text is stored as a sequence of bytes. An encoding defines how characters map to those bytes. Some encodings cover only a small set of characters, while others cover the characters of most writing systems. The same text can take a different number of bytes in different encodings.

An identifier is a value that names one thing among many. Identifiers can be numbers, words, or long strings of letters and digits. Some identifiers are random, and others are built from parts that carry a meaning. Two different things normally have two different identifiers.

A document is made of parts. A document can have a title, headings, paragraphs, figures and notes. Some documents are a single page long, and others run to hundreds of pages. The same document can exist in several file formats.

Units of measurement give a meaning to numbers. A length, a weight or a duration is expressed as a number followed by a unit. Units have symbols, such as a letter or a short group of letters. The same quantity can be expressed in different units.

A link points to a resource. The address of a link has a scheme, a host and a path, and it can also carry parameters. The text shown for a link can differ from its address. A link can point to a page, a file or a section within a page.

Images are made of pixels arranged in a grid. The size of an image is given by its width and its height. Image files come in several formats, some of which compress the data and some of which do not. An image can also carry a short description of what it shows.

Versions mark the successive states of something that changes. A version can be a number, a date or a name. Version numbers are often made of several parts separated by dots. A newer version usually comes after an older one in the sequence.

Data is kept in different kinds of storage. Some storage keeps data for a short time, and some keeps it for years. Data can be organised in folders, in tables or in collections of records. Each kind of storage has its own way of finding an item again.

Items can be arranged in many orders. An order can follow the alphabet, a date, a size or a number. The same set of items can be shown in ascending or descending order. When two items have the same value, their relative order depends on how the arrangement was made.

A calendar divides time into days, weeks, months and years. Months have different numbers of days. Weeks begin on different days depending on the region. Some calendars count years from a different starting point than others.

Characters include letters, digits, punctuation marks and symbols. Letters can be uppercase or lowercase. Some characters carry accents or other marks. Spaces and line breaks are characters too, even though they are not visible as marks on the page.

A record can accumulate a history over time. Each change to the record can be noted with the time at which it happened. A history shows the earlier states of the record next to the current one. Some histories keep every change, and others keep only the most recent ones.

Labels are short names attached to things. A label can be a single word or a few words. The same thing can carry several labels, and the same label can be attached to several things. Labels are often used to group similar items together.

Sizes of data are measured in bytes. A kilobyte, a megabyte and a gigabyte are larger units. Depending on the convention, one of these units is worth either one thousand or one thousand and twenty-four of the unit below it. A short text takes a few kilobytes at most.

A duration is the length of time between two moments. Durations can be expressed in seconds, minutes, hours or days. A duration can also be written as a combination of units, such as hours and minutes together. The same duration has the same length wherever it is measured.

Text on a page has a layout. The layout includes margins, line lengths and the spacing between paragraphs. Headings can be larger than the body text. The same text can look different when it is shown on a small screen or on a wide one.

A queue holds items that are waiting. Items join the queue at one end and leave it at the other. The length of a queue changes as items arrive and depart. Some queues give priority to certain items, which then leave earlier than items that arrived before them.

Counting gives the number of items in a group. A count is a whole number that starts at zero. Counts can be added together to give a total. When the same item appears twice in a group, it can be counted once or twice depending on what is being counted.

A page is a unit of content. A page can be printed on paper or shown on a screen. Pages can be numbered so that a reader can find them again. Long content is often divided into several pages of similar length.

Headings introduce sections. A heading is usually shorter than the text that follows it. Headings can have levels, where a section contains smaller sections with their own headings. The headings of a document, taken together, form an outline of its contents.

Spacing separates the parts of a text. A space separates words, a line break separates lines, and a blank line often separates paragraphs. Indentation moves a line further from the margin. In some formats the amount of indentation carries a meaning.

Punctuation marks include the full stop, the comma, the colon, the semicolon and the question mark. Quotation marks surround words taken from elsewhere. Parentheses enclose a remark inside a sentence. Different languages use some of these marks in different ways.

An archive gathers several files into one. Archives can be compressed so that they take less space. Opening an archive restores the files it contains, with their names and their folders. An archive can contain other archives inside it.

Clocks measure the passing of time. A clock can show hours from one to twelve or from zero to twenty-three. Two clocks in different places can show different times at the same moment. Some clocks are adjusted automatically, and others are set by hand.

A session begins when a conversation starts and ends when it stops. A session can last a few seconds or several hours. During a session, messages are exchanged in turns. Some sessions follow earlier ones, while others begin without any earlier exchange.

A result is what comes back after an operation has run. A result can be a value, a message, a file or nothing at all. Some operations return quickly, and others take longer. When an operation does not succeed, the result can describe what happened instead.

A file has a name and an extension. The extension, placed after the last dot in the name, often indicates the type of the file. Files are kept in folders, and folders can contain other folders. The full location of a file is its path.

Text can be written in many languages. Languages use different alphabets, and some use no alphabet at all. The same idea can take more or fewer words in different languages. A single text can contain words from more than one language.

A keyboard has keys for letters, digits and symbols. Some keys change the meaning of others while they are held down. Keyboard layouts differ between countries, so the same key can produce a different character. A key that stays pressed can repeat its character several times.

A screen shows pictures made of small dots of light. The number of dots across and down is the resolution of the screen. Screens come in many sizes, from a watch to a wall. The same page can occupy more or less of a screen depending on its resolution.

Colours on a screen are mixed from red, green and blue light. A colour can be written as three numbers, one for each of these lights, or as a short code of letters and digits. Two colours with close codes look alike. Some colours appear differently on different screens.

A font gives letters their shape. Some fonts have small strokes at the ends of their letters, and others do not. In some fonts every character takes the same width, which lines characters up in columns. The same text can be shown in many fonts without its words changing.

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one subject. Paragraphs are separated by a blank line or by an indented first line. Some paragraphs hold a single sentence, and others hold many. The length of a paragraph varies from one kind of text to another.

A sentence usually begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. A sentence can be a few words long or run over several lines. Short sentences and long sentences often appear side by side in the same text.

Words are separated by spaces in many languages, though not in all of them. A word can be counted, and the number of words gives one measure of the length of a text. Some words are very common and appear in almost every sentence, while others appear rarely.

An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or a phrase. Some abbreviations are made of the first letters of several words, and others keep the beginning of a single word. The same abbreviation can stand for different things in different contexts.

A quotation repeats words that were written or spoken elsewhere. Quotations are often placed between quotation marks or set apart as a separate block. A quotation can be a single word, a sentence or a longer passage. The source of a quotation is sometimes named next to it.

A footnote is a short note placed at the bottom of a page. A small number or symbol in the text points to it. Some documents gather all their notes at the end instead. Notes can hold a reference, a definition or a remark that would interrupt the main text.

An index is a list of terms placed at the end of a book. Each term is followed by the numbers of the pages where it appears. The terms of an index are arranged alphabetically. Some indexes group related terms under a common heading.

A table of contents lists the sections of a document in the order in which they appear. Each entry can carry the number of the page where its section begins. Some tables of contents show only the main sections, and others show every level of heading.

A reference list names the works that a text draws on. Each entry gives an author, a title and a date, and often more details. Reference lists follow different styles, which place these details in different orders. The same work can appear in several reference lists.

A spreadsheet arranges values in a grid of cells. Columns are usually named with letters and rows with numbers, so each cell has an address made of both. A spreadsheet file can hold several sheets. Cells can contain text, numbers, dates or nothing at all.

A cell of a spreadsheet can hold a formula instead of a plain value. A formula refers to other cells and computes its value from theirs. When a referenced cell changes, the formula shows a new value. Some formulas refer to a whole range of cells at once.

A chart shows numbers as shapes. Bars, lines, points and slices of a circle are common shapes in charts. The same numbers can be drawn as several kinds of chart. A chart often carries a title and a legend that names its series.

Many charts have two axes, one across and one up. Each axis has a scale, marked with values at regular steps. An axis can start at zero or at another value. The labels on an axis name what it measures and, often, the unit used.

A percentage expresses a part of a whole as a number out of one hundred. The same proportion can be written as a percentage, a fraction or a decimal number. Percentages can be greater than one hundred when a quantity is compared with a smaller one.

A fraction is written as one number above or before another, separated by a line or a slash. The number below the line is the denominator and the number above it is the numerator. Different fractions can stand for the same value, as one half and two quarters do.

Rounding replaces a number with a nearby number that has fewer digits. A number can be rounded to the nearest whole number, to the nearest ten or to a given number of decimal places. A rounded number is close to the original one but not always equal to it.

A negative number is less than zero. Negative numbers are usually written with a minus sign in front of them, and sometimes between parentheses. Temperatures, heights and balances can all be negative. Adding a negative number to a positive one gives a smaller result.

A range of numbers runs from a lowest value to a highest value. A range can include both of its ends, one of them or neither. Ranges are often written with a dash between their two ends. Two ranges can overlap, touch or stay apart.

An average summarizes a set of numbers with a single number. The mean adds the numbers and divides the total by how many there are. The median is the middle value once the numbers are put in order. The mean and the median of the same numbers can differ.

A map represents a place on a flat surface. Positions on a map can be given as coordinates, such as a latitude and a longitude. A map has a scale that relates distances on the map to distances on the ground. Maps can show roads, borders, rivers or heights.

A postal address names where a letter or a parcel is delivered. It can include a name, a number, a street, a town, a postal code and a country. The order of these parts differs from country to country. Some addresses also name a floor or a building.

Telephone numbers are made of digits. A number can begin with a country code, followed by an area code and a local number. Telephone numbers are written with spaces, dots or dashes between groups of digits, depending on the region. Some numbers are shorter than others.

A currency is the money used in a country or a group of countries. Each currency has a name, a symbol and a three-letter code. Amounts of money are written with a number and a symbol or code, placed before or after the number depending on the region.

A person's name can have several parts, such as a given name and a family name. The order of these parts differs between cultures. Some people have more than one given name or more than one family name. The same name can be written in different alphabets.

Some writing systems are read from left to right, and others from right to left. A few are traditionally written from top to bottom. A single page can mix texts written in both directions. The direction of a text affects where its lines begin and end.

A word in one language can have several possible equivalents in another. Some words have no exact equivalent and are explained with a phrase instead. Names of places and people are sometimes kept as they are and sometimes adapted. The same sentence can be translated in more than one way.

Alphabetical order arranges words by their letters, from the first letter onwards. Different languages place accented letters and special letters in different positions. Some lists ignore capital letters when they sort, and others place them first. Numbers in a word can be sorted as digits or as values.

Letters can be uppercase or lowercase. A text can be written entirely in capitals, in lowercase, or with capitals only at the start of sentences and names. Some identifiers treat uppercase and lowercase letters as different, and others treat them as the same.

A line of a text file can end with spaces that are not visible. Two lines that look identical can therefore differ by these trailing spaces. Some files end with an empty line, and others end directly after their last character. Tabs and spaces can both produce indentation.

Different systems mark the end of a line with different characters. One system uses a single character, and another uses a pair of characters. A file written on one system can be read on another, and its line endings may then be converted. The text itself stays the same.

A text file holds characters that can be read directly. A binary file holds bytes that only make sense to a program that knows their format. Images, archives and compiled programs are usually binary files. Opening a binary file as text shows unreadable characters.

Compression stores data in less space. Some compression keeps every detail of the original data, and some drops details that matter less. Text usually compresses well, while data that is already compressed shrinks very little. Compressed data has to be expanded before it is used.

A checksum is a short value computed from the content of a file. Two copies of a file with the same content give the same checksum. A change of a single byte usually gives a very different checksum. Checksums are written as long strings of letters and digits.

A backup is a copy of data kept apart from the original. Backups can be made every day, every week or at other intervals. Some backups copy everything, and others copy only what changed since the previous one. A backup has a date, which tells which state of the data it holds.

A copy of a file has the same content as the original when it is made. After that, the copy and the original can change separately. A copy can be kept in the same folder under another name or in another place under the same name.

Folders can contain other folders, which can contain others in turn. The depth of a folder is the number of folders above it. A path lists the folders from the top down to a file, separated by slashes or backslashes depending on the system.

A file has permissions that state who can read it, who can change it and who can run it. Permissions can differ for the owner of the file, for a group and for everyone else. The same file can be readable by many people and writable by few.

A file carries several timestamps, such as when it was created, when it was last changed and when it was last opened. These times are kept by the system that stores the file. Copying a file can keep its timestamps or replace them with the time of the copy.

Some files are hidden: they exist in a folder but are not shown in its usual listing. On some systems a file is hidden when its name starts with a dot. Hidden files often hold settings. A listing can be asked to show hidden files as well.

A temporary file holds data for a short time. Temporary files are often kept in a folder set aside for them. Some are removed when the program that made them ends, and others remain until the folder is cleared. Their names are often made of random letters and digits.

A log is a record of events written one after the other. Each line of a log often begins with a date and a time, followed by a description of the event. Logs can grow long, so they are sometimes split into several files by day or by size.

A configuration file holds settings. Many configuration files are made of keys and values, one setting per line or grouped into sections. The same setting can sometimes come from a file, from the environment or from a default value. Configuration files are usually plain text.

Many file formats allow comments: lines or parts of lines that are kept in the file but do not count as content. A comment often begins with a special character, such as a hash sign or two slashes. Comments can describe what follows or record a date.

A template is a document with a fixed structure and empty places to fill. The same template can produce many documents that look alike. The places to fill are often marked with a name between brackets or braces. A filled template no longer shows these marks.

A form gathers information through fields. Each field has a label and a place where a value is entered. Some fields accept free text, and others accept a date, a number or a choice from a list. A form can have fields that must be filled and fields that can stay empty.

Fields of a form come in several kinds. A text field accepts any characters, a list offers a set of choices, and a switch has two positions. Some fields show a hint inside them until something is entered. A field can be enabled or disabled.

A button starts an action when it is pressed. A menu lists several actions or choices, usually hidden until it is opened. Buttons and menu entries carry short labels, sometimes with a small picture. Some buttons are greyed out when their action is not available.

A window is an area of the screen that shows one program or one document. Several windows can be open at the same time, side by side or on top of each other. Inside a window, tabs can hold several pages, of which one is shown at a time.

A notification is a short message that appears to signal an event. Notifications can appear in a corner of the screen, in a list or as a sound. Some disappear after a few seconds, and others stay until they are dismissed. A notification often carries the time of its event.

An email has a sender, one or more recipients and a subject line. Its body can be plain text or formatted text, and it can carry attachments. Replies to an email often quote the earlier messages below the new text. Emails are listed by date in a mailbox.

A calendar event has a title, a start, an end and sometimes a place. Events can last part of an hour or several days. Some events repeat every week or every month. An event can involve one person or many, each of whom may accept or decline it.

The days of the week have names, which differ between languages. Some calendars number the weeks of the year from one to fifty-two or fifty-three. In some regions the week starts on Monday, and in others on Sunday or Saturday.

Most years have three hundred and sixty-five days, and a leap year has one more. The extra day is added at the end of February. Leap years usually come every four years, with a few exceptions at the turn of some centuries.

Time can be measured to a fraction of a second. A millisecond is a thousandth of a second, and a microsecond a millionth. Some records keep times to the second, and others to the millisecond. Two events recorded in the same second can still have an order.

A timer counts down from a given duration to zero. A stopwatch counts up from zero. Both show minutes and seconds, and sometimes hours or fractions of a second. A timer can be paused, resumed or reset to its starting value.

A progress indicator shows how much of a task has been done. It can be a bar that fills, a percentage or a count of steps. Some indicators know the total amount of work, and others only show that work is going on.

A task list holds items, each describing something to do. Items can be marked as done, and some lists keep done items while others hide them. A list can be ordered by date, by importance or by the order in which items were added.

Items in many systems carry a status, a short word that describes their current state. Common statuses include open, in progress and closed. An item can change status several times, and the history of those changes is sometimes kept with it.

A search box accepts words and returns the items that match them. Some searches match whole words only, and others match parts of words. Searches can ignore capital letters and accents. The results are often listed with the matching words highlighted.

A filter narrows a list down to the items that meet a condition. Several filters can be combined, and each one removes more items. Removing a filter brings its items back. The number of items left after filtering is often shown near the list.

A table on a screen can often be sorted by clicking the name of a column. A first click sorts in ascending order, and a second click in descending order. A small arrow next to the column name shows the current order.

Long lists of results are often split into pages. Each page shows a fixed number of items, and controls lead to the next page, the previous page or a page by its number. The total number of items or pages is often shown near these controls.

A tag is a short label attached to an item so that it can be found with others carrying the same label. An item can carry several tags. Tags are often shown as small rounded shapes with their text inside, sometimes in different colours.

Comments can be attached to many kinds of items. Each comment has an author, a time and a text. Comments are often shown in the order in which they were written, and replies can be grouped under the comment they answer.

A document can go through many revisions. Each revision is a saved state of the document at a given time. Two revisions can be compared to see what was added, removed or changed between them. The latest revision is usually the one shown first.
